Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/slate

# Slate

Slate is a film studio any agent can run. Every stage of a film is a `slate` command, every check is a gate, and
everything a film knows lives in its own folder, so any agent in any session can pick up exactly where the last one
stopped. This skill is the front door: it routes the request, runs intake, keeps the goal whole and hands each stage to
its craft skill.

Two words used throughout:
- **The owner** is the person Slate works for. They approve spend, the two sittings, the look, and anything published.
- **The requester** is whoever asked for this film: often the owner, sometimes someone they work with, sometimes an
  autonomous agent working for them.

## 1. Route the request before you run anything

| The request | What you do |
|---|---|
| **Open**: "make a video", "a short video of a paper boat in a storm", no length, format or brand named ("short" isn't a length), and no lane picked | Ask exactly one question, alone in its message: *"Do you want a full production or a quick generated clip?"* Run nothing and write nothing until they answer. Brand, length and format come after. |
| **Scoped**: a length, a format, a brand or a destination is named ("a 45-second launch video for …", "a 15-second 9:16 reel for …'s spring sale, captions burned in") | Straight to production (section 3). Don't ask the lane question. |
| **The quick clip, picked** (at your question, or up front: "a quick generated clip, not a full production") and no brand involved | The fast lane: hand over to Higgsfield's own skills (higgsfield-generate for a clip, higgsfield-video-explainer for a narrated explainer). No `slate new`. Mind the credits (below). |
| **Brand work**, even when it asks for "a quick Higgsfield clip" | Never the fast lane. It's a Slate production (a short express film suits it), and any generated shot runs through `slate gen` on the Cloud API: estimated, ledgered and judged against the brand's references. Say why in one line. |
| **Recording an app** to check its UI, transitions or motion (screen recordings, frame-by-frame QA, jank, flicker) | Not Slate: use video-verifier. Its web path goes through Aside, never another browser. |
| **Not a film**: web work that mentions video (a `<video>` tag, a hero video's CSS), an email, a single image | Not Slate. Do the task as the ordinary job it is. |
| **Post or publish a film** | Only a file the owner approved: its SHA-256 matches their approval and the delivery manifest marks it approved for publishing. Otherwise say which approval is missing, and stop. Slate never posts anything itself. |
| **Live action to shoot, or audio description** | Out of scope in this version. Say so, and offer what Slate can make instead. |

**Credits.** Higgsfield's skills stay installed globally because the owner uses them directly, but outside Slate they
generate on Higgsfield's app credits, a separate pool from the Cloud API balance, and that pool isn't funded by
default. If the fast lane stops for credits, say so plainly and offer a Slate production instead. Inside Slate every
generation runs on the Cloud API. Details and edge cases: [routing](references/routing.md).

## 2. Every working session starts the same way

1. **`slate status` first.** In a film folder (or with `--film <id>`) it lists every stage as fresh, stale, missing,
   locked or skipped, the sittings, open questions, locks and the one next command. Outside a film it lists the films
   on this machine. Trust it over your memory and over any summary.
2. **Snapshot the balances**, with one label for the whole session: `slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>`.
   At the end, run the same `slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>` again, then
   `slate ledger reconcile --session <label>`, so spend made through the chat connectors is caught. Slate can't read
   Higgsfield's balance itself: if a Higgsfield connector or its skills ran in the session, record that balance at
   both ends too, `slate ledger snapshot --provider higgsfield --balance <n> --session <label>`, with the number from
   the connector or the dashboard.
3. **Read `brief/GOAL.md` and `brief/PRODUCTION.md`.** After any summary or compaction, re-derive the checklist from the
   verbatim request in GOAL.md, never from memory, and assume something was lost until you've checked.
4. **Do the next thing** `slate status` names, with the skill for that stage (section 4).

## 3. Starting a film: intake

Goal fidelity comes first. The dropped requirement is never the headline; it's the aside, the "and also", the second
message.

1. **Capture every ask** in the requester's own words: split on every "and", list, comma and follow-up. Vague asks
   become intent items rather than disappearing. Restate the list back if anything is ambiguous.
2. **Check the brand**: `slate brand validate <brand>`.
   - No pack for the brand: onboarding comes first, before any script (`slate brand init <brand>`, then the
     slate-brand skill). A film looks right only when its look is built from the brand's own design system and a
     motion law measured from reference films; generic looks were rejected four times on the first film.
   - A pack whose four references (truth, look and motion, voice, sound) aren't all approved: finish onboarding with
     `slate brand onboard <brand>` before the script. The neutral `demo` pack is the exception: it exists for trials,
     tests and demos, and its look test rides in the film's pre-production sitting.
   - Autonomous films refuse any brand without all four references approved.
3. **Choose the format** from Slate's templates (reel, ad, explainer, brand film and the rest: [formats](references/formats.md);
   each is a JSON file in Slate's `formats/` folder, named for the format). The format sets runtime, aspect, pace,
   structure, loudness, captions and safe zones.
4. **Settle mode, generation and budget** ([modes](references/modes.md), [budgets](references/budgets.md)): supervised
   unless the requester says otherwise; generation `rarely` unless they ask for more or none.
5. **Make the film**, with the request verbatim:
   ```
   slate new <film-id> --brand <brand> --format <format> --request "<the request, word for word>" --source "<who asked>"
   ```
   Add `--mode`, `--generation`, `--runtime` or `--aspect` when the brief sets them; `--request-file` takes a long
   request from a file. This writes film.json (clock, size, budget, mode), `brief/GOAL.md` (the request and a checklist
   of every ask) and `brief/PRODUCTION.md`, and starts the film's git history.
6. **Record later messages** the same way, verbatim. GOAL.md names the commands that add a message and mark an ask
   done; done always needs evidence.
7. **Go as far as asked.** When the requester says how far to take it ("as far as the script"), stop there and name
   what comes next, usually the pre-production sitting.

Intake in depth: [intake](references/intake.md).

## 4. The production, stage by stage

| # | Stage | Skill | Commands | Who approves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Brand onboarding (once per brand) | slate-brand | `slate brand init`, `slate brand onboard`, `slate analyze`, `slate brand approve` | the owner approves four references |
| 1 | Brief | slate (this) | `slate new` | pre-production sitting |
| 2 | Truth: sources, claims, sample data | slate-story | `brief/truth.json`, `slate script build` | pre-production sitting (claims) |
| 3 | Treatment and script | slate-story | `script/script.json`, `slate script build` | pre-production sitting |
| 4 | Voice: cast or design, then every line | slate-voice | `slate voice cast`, `slate voice design`, `slate voice tts` | shortlist at the sitting |
| 5 | Timing | slate-story | `slate timing` | none: frame-exact or nothing is written |
| 6 | Look test (skipped when the brand's look is approved) | slate-motion, slate-brand | `slate render` of a short test | pre-production sitting |
| 7 | Kit, builders' brief, acts, captures | slate-build | `slate emit-events`, `slate check`, `slate capture ios` | hero moments, in the packet |
| 8 | Generated shots (only where allowed) | slate-generate | `slate plates plan`, `slate gen run` | takes, in the packet |
| 9 | Score, sound and mix | slate-sound | `slate score plan`, `slate mix`, `slate verify` | sound proofs, in the packet |
| 10 | Render with true motion blur | slate-finish | `slate render` | none: gates |
| 11 | Master | slate-finish | `slate master --ae` (supervised, on the owner's go) or `slate master --ffmpeg` | the owner starts the AE finish |
| 12 | Validate and deliver | slate-qa, slate-finish | `slate qa`, `slate deliver` | final-cut sitting |
| 13 | Review and correct | slate-finish, slate-qa | `slate review`, the same gates again | the owner's notes |

`slate make <target>` rebuilds only what's stale, in order. The method behind the table, with every machine gate, is in
[orchestration](references/orchestration.md); the stages are one clock, so a re-voice re-times everything downstream.

**Parallel work.** If you can run sub-agents, build acts in parallel, one builder per act under one brief; otherwise
build them in order. Either way a builder owns only its act's files, gets a first working version of every shot onto
disk fast, and keeps its NOTES.md current (slate-build).

## 5. Sittings, packets and approvals

- **Two sittings block a supervised film.** The pre-production sitting approves the checklist, the claims, the script,
  the voice shortlist and the look test. The final-cut sitting approves the film. Stop and hand over at each one:
  finish the packet, say plainly what's waiting for them, and don't start the next stage.
- **Packets don't block.** Hero moments, generated takes and sound proofs arrive in review packets the owner answers
  when they like; keep working on everything that doesn't depend on them.
- **An approval is bound to exact bytes.** Record each one with the command `slate status` names for it: it stores
  the SHA-256 of what was approved, so a changed file is no longer approved. Approved takes, score takes, plates and the
  final cut are locked by hash and never regenerated without an explicit force and a spend approval.
- **Only a person approves.** Never record an approval on anyone's behalf, never read approval into silence, and never
  treat a REVIEW verdict as a pass. Voices, sound and looks are picked by ear and eye; your measurements only shortlist.
- **Asking for a decision:** name it in one line, then ask a few concrete sub-questions whose answers settle it (their
  situation, their preference in practice, the edge case). If your agent has an interactive question tool, use it.
  Then say which way the answers point, and read free-text answers literally.

More: [approvals](references/approvals.md).

## 6. Budgets and spend

- Every paid call goes through Slate's ledger: estimate, budget check, an in-flight row with its request id, then the
  result. `slate budget show` has the month and each film's budget; `slate ledger list` has every paid call.
- A film's budget is a hard stop. 1.5 times is allowed only for marked rework. Spending past it needs the owner's
  recorded yes, and an autonomous film can never raise its own.
- **Slate never buys credits, upgrades a plan or starts a licence.** When a balance runs out, the work stops and asks.
- An optional extra that costs real credits (a dedicated score swell is about 1,100 to 1,500) is offered with its price
  and made only on the owner's yes, even when the budget would cover it.
- Replay is the default for tests and demos (`SLATE_FAKE_VENDORS=1`); `--live` spends for real.

Default budgets by format: [budgets](references/budgets.md).

## 7. Modes

- **Supervised** (the default): both sittings block; spend past the film's budget asks first; After Effects finishes
  it on the owner's go.
- **Express**: a short film runs straight to a review cut, and every approval is batched into the final-cut sitting.
- **Draft**: no generated plates, a library voice, fewer motion-blur samples. For animatics and quick variants. Never
  delivered as final.
- **Autonomous** (agents working for the owner): approved brands and approved claims only, every generation waits for
  the owner's yes, no After Effects, a separate reviewer grades the cut before it parks, and every output stays "not
  approved for publishing" until the owner approves that exact file.

The full rules: [modes](references/modes.md).

## 8. The tracker

`brief/GOAL.md` holds the request verbatim and the checklist of every ask; `brief/PRODUCTION.md` holds the asks,
every direction change (numbered and quoted exactly), open questions, revisions, approvals and the status table. Slate
keeps the blocks between its markers current; write anything else around them. Status words mean one thing each:
**done** is verified with named evidence; a proof is not a finished shot. `slate status --write` refreshes the table.
See [tracker](references/tracker.md).

## 9. Perfect, don't replace

When the owner approves something and adds notes, the notes are perfecting notes. Apply them to that exact artifact,
keep everything else as it was, and check the revision against the approved version by measurement (levels against
the voice, sync, palette). A note that seems to need a new approach gets a question first. Research only fixes a named
flaw; it never becomes a redesign. (One film's sound went off the rails exactly this way: small notes were answered
with a new sound system, and the effects that had stood out ended up buried.) `slate revise start <file> --notes …
--by <name>` turns the notes into a checklist of changes to that file, `slate revise check` measures the revision
against the approved version, and `slate revise done` refuses to close while anything else moved.
See [review and correct](references/review-and-correct.md).

## 10. Resilience

A production can run for days and outlive every agent that works on it.
- Everything a film knows is in its folder; `slate status` tells any agent where it stands.
- Long work (renders, masters, word timings, score composition, generation batches) runs as detached jobs in the
  queue: `--detach` returns a job id at once; follow it with `slate job status <id>`, `slate job wait <id>` and
  `slate job log <id>`. A dying agent, a sleeping Mac or a rate limit doesn't lose it: a job turned away by a vendor's
  rate limit (exit 75) goes back in the queue and tries again after the vendor's own wait.
- **Nothing prompts.** Research slices are killed after ten minutes with stdin as a pipe, so never start anything that
  waits for input. Keys are typed by a person in their own Terminal with `slate connect`, never in chat.
- **Inside the OpenClaw gateway, every paid stage is a job.** The gateway's egress proxy blocks the vendors, and the
  job runner works outside it: run voicing, music and generation with `--detach` or `slate job submit`, never inline
  ([agents and connectors](references/agents-and-connectors.md)).
- Save early and often: a session can end without warning.

See [resilience](references/resilience.md).

## 11. Protections

- **Voices:** designed or library voices by default; the owner's own voice only as a professional clone they verified
  themselves; anyone else's only as a real recording, never a clone, and never a public figure's.
- **People and claims:** no invented testimonials or customer quotes presented as real, and no claim without a source.
- **AI labels:** none unless the law requires one. Slate still records which voices and shots are synthetic, internally,
  and platform rules on realistic AI voices or people are the owner's call per platform.
- **Company material:** company source code is read in place and never copied; brand material goes to a generator only
  when the brand owner allows it.
- **Spend:** never buy, never upgrade, never call a vendor's tool that uploads a user's skills or profile.
- **Browsers:** never open a web browser. Read the web with fetch and search tools; any page that must be driven goes
  through Aside.

The why behind each: [protections](references/protections.md).

## 12. Helpers, vendor skills, licences

- **Optional helpers:** ponder as a QA loop over every shot; visionary for hero moments; goal-fidelity for the
  checklist; asset-creator (vector drawing), canvas-design (frames), frontend-design (component looks) and
  avoid-ai-writing (script polish). None is required; Slate works without them.
- **Vendor skills:** Remotion's and ElevenLabs' skills live inside Slate's engine folder, not globally, and Slate's
  rules override theirs where they disagree. Higgsfield's stay global. Slate never deletes a vendor skill; if one keeps
  winning a request Slate should get, adjust Slate's own trigger with the owner's one-time permission.
- **Code you never copy:** OpenMontage is AGPL, and copying its code would force that licence on Slate. Ideas only.
  Licences in depth: [licences](references/licences.md).

## Reference files

- [routing](references/routing.md): every routing case, the one question, the fast lane and its credits.
- [intake](references/intake.md): capturing the brief, re-deriving the checklist, the brand check.
- [formats](references/formats.md): the format templates and derived films.
- [modes](references/modes.md): supervised, express, draft and autonomous, rule by rule.
- [approvals](references/approvals.md): sittings, packets, what counts as approval, asking for decisions.
- [budgets](references/budgets.md): default budgets, the ledger, never buying.
- [tracker](references/tracker.md): GOAL.md, PRODUCTION.md, status words, direction changes.
- [orchestration](references/orchestration.md): the method as a workflow, parallel builders, production routes.
- [review-and-correct](references/review-and-correct.md): review packets, notes, targeted fixes, versions.
- [resilience](references/resilience.md): detached jobs, sessions that end, files agents read.
- [protections](references/protections.md): voices, claims, labels, company material, spend, browsers.
- [agents-and-connectors](references/agents-and-connectors.md): the agents, the CLI, MCP, the chat lane.
- [dependencies](references/dependencies.md): tools, vendor skills, optional helpers, checking a tool first.
- [licences](references/licences.md): Remotion, Adobe, Eleven Music, ElevenLabs plans, AGPL code, fonts, sounds.
- [research](references/research.md): reading vendor docs, dated sources, the web without a browser.

`slate guide <topic>` prints these same files for an agent that can't read the skill folder.

# Intake: the brief, in the requester's own words

Intake turns a request into a film folder with the goal written down exactly as it was asked. Everything later is
checked against that record, so it has to be complete and verbatim.

## 1. Capture every ask

Big requests get half-delivered when one ask quietly drops out. It's almost never the headline; it's the aside, the
subordinate clause, the "oh, and also" at the end, the second message an hour later.

- Split the request on every "and", "also", "plus", list item and comma-separated clause.
- Write implied deliverables out: "a reel with captions for Instagram and TikTok" is a reel, burned-in captions, and
  two platforms' safe zones.
- Keep vague asks as intent items ("make it feel less corporate") instead of dropping them because they aren't crisp.
- Carry open threads: a question the requester asked that nobody has answered yet is an ask too.
- If anything is ambiguous, restate the list back so they can correct it.

## 2. Write it down verbatim

```
slate new <film-id> --brand <brand> --format <format> --request "<the request, word for word>" --source "<who asked>"
```

- `--request` takes the words exactly as they arrived, typos included. `--request-file <path>` reads a long one.
- `brief/GOAL.md` then holds the request, a checklist row per ask (auto-split rows are flagged for you to check) and the
  settings rows (format, brand, budget, mode). `brief/PRODUCTION.md` is the live tracker (see tracker.md).
- Every later message that adds or changes an ask goes in verbatim too, with who sent it. GOAL.md names the command.
- If the original request was cut off or summarized away, say so in the tracker, and mark any ask you rebuilt from
  follow-ups as reconstructed.

**After any summary or compaction, re-derive the checklist from the verbatim request, never from memory.** Summaries
drop sub-requirements; assume something was lost and go find it.

## 3. Check the brand

`slate brand validate <brand>` reports the pack and which of its four references are approved.

| What you find | What happens |
|---|---|
| No pack for this brand | Onboarding first (`slate brand init <brand>`, then slate-brand). No script before it. |
| A pack with references still unapproved | Finish onboarding (`slate brand onboard <brand>`) before the script. |
| The neutral `demo` pack | Go ahead: it's for trials, tests and demos; its look test rides in the film's pre-production sitting. |
| All four references approved | Go ahead. T
[… 4,387 characters left out of the recording …]
rated plates, a library voice, fewer motion-blur samples (4 instead of 16).
- For animatics, quick variants and trying an idea.
- **Never delivered as final.** A draft that becomes the real thing leaves draft mode and goes through the gates again.

## Autonomous (agents working for the owner, such as Oneiro's pursuits)

- **Brands:** only brands whose four references are approved.
- **Claims:** only from the brand's approved-claims list. A new claim parks the film with a question for the owner.
- **REVIEW verdicts park the film** with their evidence, and never count as passes. Only a person releases it.
- **Spend** is capped monthly in Slate's own budget file, which the CLI enforces whatever film.json says, and backed by
  vendor caps: a separate ElevenLabs key for autonomous work, with its own credit quota. An autonomous film can't raise
  its own budget.
- **Every generation waits for the owner's yes**, asked by iMessage, recorded, and passed to the run as an approval id.
- **No After Effects.** Autonomous films are mastered with ffmpeg and held. The owner can start the AE finish
  themselves once they approve the held film: a final-cut approval of its held master, then `slate master --ae --go` in
  their own Terminal (never queued, never `--detach`). No agent starts it.
- **Voices:** the owner's own professional clone is the only clone it may use.
- **Default output:** a 15 to 45 second 9:16 reel.
- **Before parking,** a separate reviewer agent grades the contact sheet and the audio against the brand's references,
  the owner's taste notes and the visionary bar (slate-qa, reviewer-agent.md).
- **Not approved for publishing:** every output says so in its manifest until the owner approves that exact SHA-256.
  After their yes, the agent posts that exact file through its own committing path, and never any other version.
- **Denied tools:** publishing through a vendor connector (TikTok, website publishing) and any tool that uploads the
  user's skills or a personality profile to a vendor.
- **Held films and questions** reach the owner by iMessage, with the phone cut, and as a push notification.

## Choosing a mode

| Situation | Mode |
|---|---|
| The owner (or someone they work with) is making a film and wants to steer it | supervised |
| A short piece, and they'd rather react to a cut than approve a script | express |
| Trying an idea, an animatic, a variant to compare | draft |
| An agent working on the owner's behalf, on an approved brand | autonomous |

# Formats: what "any video" means in practice

A format is a template in Slate's `formats/` folder. It sets the runtime, aspect and size, frame rate, pace, structure,
loudness target, caption defaults, per-platform safe zones and the default budget. `slate new --format <name>` copies
its values into film.json, which is then the one source of the film's clock and size. Nothing downstream assumes a
frame size or rate; everything reads film.json.

| Format | Runtime | Aspect | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brand film | 2 to 6 minutes | 16:9 | The long form: several acts, a composed score, the AE finish when supervised. |
| Explainer | 60 to 120 seconds | 16:9 (or 9:16) | One idea, told clearly; 0 to 2 generated shots at most. |
| Product demo | 30 to 120 seconds | per destination | Real app captures through `slate capture ios` or `slate capture web`. Capture for truth and speed; rebuild in code when a shot needs camera moves, restaging, motion blur or exact type. |
| Social reel | 15 to 45 seconds | 9:16 | Captions burned in by the renderer in the brand's font. Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Shorts. The autonomous default. |
| Ad | 6, 15 or 30 seconds | 16:9, 1:1 or 9:16 | Every second counts: one idea, one call to action. |
| LinkedIn cut | 15 to 60 seconds | 1:1 and 4:5 | Usually derived from a larger film. |
| Website hero loop | per page | per page | Loops seamlessly; no voice; to the platform's spec. |
| App Store preview | to the store's spec | device | The store's size, length and safe areas. |
| Launch teaser or feature announcement | 10 to 45 seconds | any | A single reveal, often a signature moment and a sting. |
| Kinetic type or logo sting | 3 to 15 seconds | any | Type-led; the editorial look or the logo build. |
| Character-led | any | any | The brand's motif or mark as a character (slate-motion, character-and-motif-motion). |

The format files are the source of truth for exact values; this table is the overview. `slate formats list` names them
all, and `slate formats show <name> [--aspect 9:16]` gives one in full: its runtime and clock, the read time and the
planning rate the script gates use, its caption rules at that aspect, its channels and their safe zones, its budget,
and the platform files `slate deliver` makes for it (each platform's size, clock and limits).

## Derived films: cut-downs, aspects and languages

A cut-down, a new aspect or a new language is a **derived film** with a parent. It reuses the parent's approved takes,
timings, beats a
[… 3,241 characters left out of the recording …]
ag A/Bs included); score 9,000 to 28,000 | $40 to 85 | |
| Brand onboarding (once) | Voice Design about 5,000 | $15 to 20 for look tests | The sound reference is made locally. |

For scale: a code-only film spends nothing on generation; a hybrid film with about 40 seconds of generated plates, a
few takes each, spent roughly $8 to 30; an all-generated six-minute cut would be roughly $55 to 95.

## Spend Slate can't see

Generations made in a chat through the hosted connectors (Higgsfield's or ElevenLabs') bypass the ledger. The ledger
catches them by comparing balance snapshots:

```
slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>        # at the start of a working session
slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>        # at the end, with the same label
slate ledger reconcile --session <label>
```

`--all` records every balance Slate can read by itself (ElevenLabs'); it skips Higgsfield, which has no balance
endpoint. When a Higgsfield connector or Higgsfield's own skills ran in the session, record its balance at both ends
from the connector's balance tool or the dashboard:

```
slate ledger snapshot --provider higgsfield --balance <n> --session <label>
```

A reconcile that finds unexplained spend is REVIEW, for the owner to look at. A provider with only one snapshot in the
session is UNCHECKED, never a pass.

## Two wallets at Higgsfield

The **Cloud API** balance pays for every Slate generation and is the one funded lane. **App credits** pay for
Higgsfield's CLI, app and hosted connector, including its own skills; that pool isn't funded by default, so the fast
lane may stop for credits. Neither is ever topped up by an agent.

Cloud API credit expires a year after it's bought; app-plan credits expire every billing cycle. When the owner buys
Cloud API credit, it's for the films actually planned, never ahead of them.

## Watching spend during a film

- `slate ledger list --film <id>` has every paid call for the film; `slate ledger inflight` shows calls still waiting.
- Before a batch (a full voicing, a score, several takes), say what it will cost and what's left of the budget.
- An optional extra that costs real credits (a dedicated score swell is about 1,100 to 1,500 credits) is offered with
  its price and made only on the owner's yes, even when the budget would cover it.
- Before spending past an approval (a recomposition, a re-voice of approved lines), try what's on hand first: an unused
  take often measures better than a new one, and costs nothing.

# Routing: getting every video request to the right place

Slate claims any request to make, edit, plan or review a video. Higgsfield's skills also claim "make a video", so the
front door has to win the request and then send it to the right lane. Routing evals check this in every agent (Claude
Code, Codex, a pursuit slice, OpenClaw): open requests get the question, scoped briefs load Slate, UI recordings still go
to video-verifier, and unrelated requests never load Slate.

## What counts as a video request

Explainers, ads, social reels, promos, launch and feature announcements, teasers, product demos, brand films, website
hero loops, App Store previews, kinetic type, logo stings, character-led pieces, cut-downs and new aspects of a film,
voice-overs and captions for a film, a review of a cut, and delivering or posting a finished film.

What doesn't count, even when the word "video" appears:
- styling, embedding or debugging a `<video>` element or a hero video's CS
[… 2,883 characters left out of the recording …]
 production, where a generated shot runs on the Cloud API
with an estimate first.

**Never for brand work.** A brand's film goes through Slate even when the ask says "a quick Higgsfield clip for
<brand>'s launch". Stylized generated clips aren't the brand's type, colour or real UI, and the fast lane skips truth,
claims, the ledger and take judging. Say that in one line, then run a short production: express mode suits it, with
`--generation where-it-helps` when the requester wants generated footage.

## UI recordings go to video-verifier

"Screen-record the sign-up flow in the Simulator and check the transitions frame by frame" is QA of an app, not a film.
Load video-verifier, not Slate. Its web recordings go through Aside, never another browser.

A **product demo film** that uses real app footage is Slate's: the footage comes from `slate capture ios` or
`slate capture web`, conformed to the film's clock and beat-mapped to the voice (slate-build).

## Editing and reviewing

- **Editing a Slate film:** notes on approved work are a revision of that exact artifact (perfect, don't replace); a
  cut-down, a new aspect or a new language is a derived film (slate-finish).
- **Editing an outside video:** `slate analyze <video>` breaks it down (transcript, scenes, measured eases); then either
  rebuild it as a Slate film or, for a trivial trim, make the trim and say that's all it was.
- **Reviewing a cut:** a Slate film's review packet comes from `slate review`; an outside film gets `slate analyze` and
  the review checklist in slate-qa.

## Posting and publishing

Nothing publishes itself. A request to post a film is refused unless the owner approved that exact file: its SHA-256
matches their approval, and the delivery manifest marks it approved for publishing. When either is missing, say exactly
which approval is missing and stop. Don't upload it anywhere, don't open a site to post it, and don't take any other
committing action on the requester's behalf.

## Out of scope in this version

Shooting live action, and audio description. Say so, then offer what Slate can make: a film from real app captures,
generated real-world shots where the generation setting allows, or captions and a transcript.

## When a vendor skill keeps winning

If Higgsfield's (or any vendor's) skill keeps taking requests Slate should get, adjust Slate's own trigger (the skill
descriptions), with the owner's one-time permission, and re-run the routing evals. Never delete or edit a vendor skill.

Generation runs only on the Higgsfield Cloud API (the one funded lane), only where the film's generation

their yes; slate gen run --shot S05 --approval <id> spends.

Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/slate-story

# slate-story

The story is data. One hand-edited file, `script/script.json`, holds every act and shot: what the voice says, what's on
screen, what the picture does, and where every claim comes from. `slate script build` checks it through the script
gates and writes the storyboard and a readable SCRIPT.md, and it refuses to write anything while a gate fails. Nothing
downstream is typed by hand: shot lengths, timecodes and frames all come from this file and the voice's real reads.

This skill covers stages 2 (truth), 3 (treatment and script) and 5 (timing) of the production. The front door (the
slate skill) has already made the film folder and the brief.

## 1. Truth first

Before a line is written, know what's true and who says so.
- The **brand's truth** (from onboarding): its claim authority, sources, approved claims, never-claim list, banned
  words and sample data.
- The **film's truth pack**, `brief/truth.json`: the sources this film relies on, each pinned (a commit, a retrieval
  date or a hash), the researched claims that cite them, what this film never claims, and its sample data.
- The product's own code, read in place at a pinned commit, is the only product truth: it wins over docs, demos,
  prototypes and older films. The owner's rulings win over the code for what's claimed.

Every claim and every number said or shown must be on the brand's approved list or cite a pinned source. Autonomous
films use approved claims only. Research method and templates: [truth](references/truth.md). The rules every frame and
line obeys: [truth packs](references/truth-packs.md).

## 2. The treatment

For anything longer than a short ad, write a treatment before the script: the idea as a reframe, why this runtime, act
by act, the emotional arc, one signature moment per act, the voice and the look and the sound in a line each, what the
film never shows, and the owner's calls so far. Keep it to a page or two. Template and craft:
[treatment](references/treatment.md); story shapes that work: [structure](references/structure.md).

## 3. The script as data

Write `script/script.json`: acts of shots, each with an id, the VO line, the on-screen words, the picture, the
transition out, and its sources and claims. Shape, fields and a worked example: [script as data](references/script-as-data.md).

```
slate script build --check      # the gates only; writes nothing
slate script build              # gates, then script/storyboard.json and script/SCRIPT.md
```

The gates: schema, structure, pace (2.6 words a second or less, per shot), read time, on-screen density, runtime
(within 10% of the target), banned words (VO, on screen and picture), claims, numbers, quotes (no invented testimonial),
sources, and the shot-id freeze. A failure lists what to fix; fix the script, never the generated files.
`storyboard.json` and `SCRIPT.md` say "generated: do not edit by hand".

Shot ids freeze when the build passes; once scenes use them, a renumber is refused. Add shots with new ids instead.

## 4. Writing the voice-over

- **Pace:** at most 2.6 words a second, per shot. Plan shot lengths from the words, then let the real reads re-time
  them (section 6).
- **Read time:** every on-screen statement holds, once fully built, at least max(1.5 s, 0.4 s + 0.3 s per word);
  numbers hold 2 s after they land.
- **Density:** at most 12 on-screen words per shot; on-screen text is keywords (about 40% of what the voice says or
  less), never a transcript of the VO.
- **Numbers and symbols** are written the way they're spoken or shown consistently; the clock knows how "664" or "&" is
  said, so word lookups find them.
- **Brand words** go in the brand's lexicon, so the voice checks can hear them said in full.
- **The words are final before voicing.** Direction (tone, pauses) is added later as audio tags that never change a
  word (slate-voice).

More craft, with the fixes for each gate: [VO writing](references/vo-writing.md).

## 5. The visionary bar

Make beautiful things that would make someone cry. Every act gets **one signature moment**: the beat people remember,
built inside the brand's own visual language (no glows, flares, particles or bounce). A correct but ordinary animation
doesn't meet the bar. If the visionary skill is available, use it before designing any hero moment: reframe, go wide
across lenses, kill the median, push one idea to a signature. Mark each act's moment in the treatment and in the script
(the shot's `notes`), so builders know where the film's weight is. See [signature moments](references/signature-moments.md).

## 6. After voicing: the clock

Once the takes are approved (slate-voice):
```
slate script build --from-takes     # every voiced shot re-timed from its approved take
slate timing                        # shots, voice cues, word timings, events, timeline on the film's clock
```
- `slate timing` writes `timing/shots.json`, `vo_cues.json`, `vo_words.json`, `events.json` and `timeline.json`. It
  refuses to write unless the frames are exact and contiguous.
- Word timings come from Whisper by default; a word lookup never throws, it falls back to an estimate and records a
  miss. The miss list must be empty before any act is handed in (slate-build).
- Once an act render is registered the timing locks; only the owner can decide to re-time, with a reason.

## 7. Handing over to the pre-production sitting

When the script builds clean (and the treatment, the truth pack and the voice shortlist are ready), stop. The
pre-production sitting approves the checklist, the claims, the script, the voice shortlist and, when the brand's look
isn't approved, the look test. Say what's ready, where it is (SCRIPT.md, the truth pack, the casting reel), and what
each decision is. Record the owner's calls on the draft (trims, keeps, confirmations) as numbered decisions in the
tracker, with their words.

## Rules that hold everywhere

- One hand-edited source. Never edit storyboard.json, SCRIPT.md or the timing files; change script.json and rebuild.
- Nothing is invented: every UI element, word and number maps to a citation (truth packs).
- No invented testimonials or customer quotes presented as real; quotes carry who said them and a pinned source.
- Runtime stays within 10% of the target unless the requester asks otherwise or you justify it in the tracker.
- The picture can be restaged freely by builders; the words, beats and timing are the script's.

## References

- [truth](references/truth.md): researching truth; pinned sources; product-truth and capability-brief templates.
- [truth-packs](references/truth-packs.md): the rules every line and frame obeys about claims, data and the product.
- [treatment](references/treatment.md): the treatment template and how to write each part.
- [structure](references/structure.md): story shapes that work: bookends, payoffs, journeys, the end card.
- [script-as-data](references/script-as-data.md): script.json field by field, a worked example, the gates and fixes.
- [vo-writing](references/vo-writing.md): pace, read time, density, numbers, brand words, a character's own words.
- [signature-moments](references/signature-moments.md): the visionary bar and one signature moment per act.

# Truth packs: the rules every line and frame obeys

A truth pack is the brand's truth (from onboarding) plus the film's (`brief/truth.json`). The script gates, the claims
gate and the banned-word gate read it; these rules are what it's for. Builders follow them too: the picture can make
claims just as the voice can.

## Nothing invented

- Every UI element, word and number on screen maps to a citation. Never show UI the product doesn't have.
- A concept screen (something that isn't built) needs the requester's explicit sign-off and a visible "concept"
  treatment.
- Never show a feature the product doesn't have, even if the script asks for it (a download, an integration that reads
  someone else's data). A correction from the requester removes it everywhere it appears.
- Never show as working anything that isn't built, is stubbed, or is off by default.
- Product names follow the product's current code, not older materials.
- When the product won't do something, show the absence (the empty page is the point) and draw nothing that implies
  the missing feature (no dial, gauge or projected number).

## Data

- Data graphics are drawn from the product's real distributions, ranges and clamps, never invented shapes.
- Illustrative graphics that aren't real data carry an "illustration" treatment and never show fabricated percentages.
- Conceptual charts carry no numbers and no axis labels.
- Future or illustrative data points carry no numbers; only real sample readings are labelled.
- A counter for a vague quantity (the voice says "thousands") runs as time and never settles on a precise number.
- Show aggregated data the way the product aggregates it; never single out an individual.
- When sample data must be split in ways the screen never shows, choose the split so every statement on screen stays
  true.

## Sample data

- The film's sample company, people and numbers come from one sample-data record, used everywhere.
- The sample-data label appears on every frame that shows sample data, and only there (not on frames showing product
  facts).
- The label sits in one corner for the whole film, a corner no character or UI element uses (when one does, move the
  label once, film-wide), and it lives at the act's top level, fading in with the first sample data: inside a sub-layer
  it goes missing for whole shots and then pops in. The kit's `CornerLabel` takes the corner.
- When real content isn't available (assessment questions, customer records), abstract it (word
[… 2,604 characters left out of the recording …]
 can play the opening's construction in reverse, or return to the composition the film
  opened on, with the call to action landing where the opening's first word landed.
- **The end card carries the call to action in text** as well as in the voice, and holds long enough to read twice.
- **Open out of silence** and let the first image establish the world before the first word.

## Payoffs

- **Set up a payoff visibly.** Show what's missing now (an empty dashed slot beside the thing nobody measures) and fill
  it later in the film. The viewer remembers the gap.
- **The product's own empty state** (a placeholder before the first reading) is a truthful setup for a reveal that pays
  it off.
- **Answer the viewer's "what does it do for me?"** in one object they can hold, with a page for every door it opens.
- **Leave a decision visibly to the viewer**: the last box stays empty, and nobody on screen touches it.

## Making a process into a story

- Turn a product's steps into a story about one person (the sample user decides, commits, discovers), so a process
  reads as a journey rather than a feature list.
- Follow the product's real journey order; a film that jumps around the product teaches the wrong model of it.
- Stage only what the voice names: three spoken items get three taps, not twelve.

## Remaking or answering an earlier film

- When a film is modelled on an original, follow it topic for topic, then rebuild every graphic in the current craft:
  the original's content in the new film's look.
- Recover the original's exact on-screen content by grabbing its frames (`slate analyze <video>`), not from memory or
  summaries.
- Check every claim in the original against the current product and site; the new film carries only what's still true
  (truth.md).

## Acts

- Every act has one job, one carrier (the object it's about) and one signature moment.
- An act break with no voice for a couple of seconds is a natural breath: the score can open there.
- Hand acts to each other on carries (an object that continues across), never on a cut to a title card.

## Words on screen and words in the voice

- On-screen text is keywords, not a transcript: about 40% of the words the voice says in that shot, or fewer.
- When the script's picture notes and its on-screen column disagree on wording, the on-screen column's words go on
  screen.
- The on-screen word budget (12 per shot) can justify leaving product elements out of a shot; record the omission in the
  act's notes.

## Fields

**The script:** `title`; `version` (a change note for this draft, in words); `language`; optional `timing` overrides
(`lead`, `tail`, `act_tail`, `speech_rate`, `max_pace`) and `rules` (this film's own extra rules: `vo_dashes`,
`first_line`, `every_shot_sourced`, `on_scree

| `generate` | Only for a shot that may be generated (slate-generate): a reason category and what it needs. |

## The gates

| Gate | What it checks | The usual fix |
|---|---|---|
| `script.schema` | the file's shape | the message names the field |
| `script.structure` | acts and shots are there, ids unique | add or rename shots |
| `script.pace` | 2.6 words a second or less per shot | cut words, or give the shot more time |
| `script.read_time` | every on-screen line holds max(1.5 s, 0.4 s + 0.3 s per word) once settled; numbers 2 s | fewer words on screen, or a longer shot |
| `script.on_screen` | at most 12 on-screen words per shot, and at most 40% of the words the voice says in it (words the voice says as they show are read along; a `reading` declaration answers for the rest) | keywords, not a transcript |
| `script.hero_lines` | a hero line has at most 6 words, and an act shows at most 2 | shorten it, or let one of them be body type |
| `script.runtime` | within 10% of the format's target | planning lengths (`dur`), or cut or add a beat |
| `script.banned_words` | the brand's banned words in the VO, on screen and in the picture notes | rephrase |
| `script.claims` | every claim approved or cited to a pinned source; nothing from the never-claim list | cite it, get it approved, or cut it |
| `script.numbers` | every number said or shown has a source | cite it or drop it |
| `script.quotes` | no one quoted without a named person and a pinned source; every quoted product fact still where it says it is at the pinned commit | source it or cut it; fix the `where` the message names |
| `script.sources` | sources exist and are pinned (when the film requires every shot sourced) | add the source to the truth pack |
| `script.first_line`, `script.vo_dashes` | this film's own rules, when set | as the message says |
| `script.shot_ids` | ids freeze at a clean build; a renumber is refused once scenes use them | add new ids instead of renumbering |

`slate script build --check` runs the gates and writes nothing. A failing build writes nothing either, and the last
good storyboard stays as it was.

## After voicing

`slate script build --from-takes` re-times every voiced shot from its approved take (the read plus the lead and tail)
and switches the film to take timing, which later builds keep. Shots without a take keep their planning lengths. Then
`slate timing` builds the clock (SKILL.md, section 6).

# slate-generate

Generated shots can lift a film or cheapen it. On the first films, generated pixels where code or real footage belonged
read as AI and were rejected; generated atmosphere, used carefully, earned its place. So Slate generates rarely by
default, only what code can't make, judges every take, and never ships an ugly one.

This is stage 8 of the production. Every generation runs on the Higgsfield **Cloud API** (the one funded lane), through
Slate's ledger, estimated first.

## 1. When to generate

- **The requester decides how much**: each film has a generation setting, `none`, `rarely` (the default) or
  `where-it-helps`.
- **Code first for anything designed**: UI, type, data, charts, logos and brand graphics are drawn by code, always. A
  generated plate never carries UI, text, charts or logos.
- **Generation is for what code can't make**: real-looking people, a real place or scene, a stock-style shot. On
  `where-it-helps` it can also be used where it genuinely adds something, or as a matte (its shape only), each with a
  written reason.
- **Drafts use no plates.** Autonomous films may generate under the same rules, but every generation waits for the
  owner's yes.
- **Generated people on screen need the requester's sign-off**, and a generated shot never implies a claim or a
  testimonial.

See [policy](references/policy.md).

## 2. Ask for it in the script

A shot that may be generated carries a `generate` block in `script/script.json`:

```json
"generate": {"reason": "real-scene", "why": "a real coastline at dawn, which code can't draw",
             "prompt": "…", "duration": 5, "image": "refs/start.png", "takes": 2}
```

`reason` is one of `real-people`, `real-scene`, `stock`, `adds-something`, `bridge-matte`; `contains` must list nothing
designed. File inputs are film-relative paths, `take:<shot>` (another shot's approved take) or `brand:<path>` (a file in
the brand pack, sent only when the brand allows uploads).

## 3. Plan, estimate, generate, judge, pick, conform

```
slate plates plan                          # every generate block: allowed or not and why, the model, takes, the estimate
slate gen estimate --shot S05              # the free estimate for this shot's takes
slate gen run --shot S05                   # at least two takes, each submitted once, ledger row first
slate gen judge --shot S05                 # a contact sheet and numbers for each take, and a REVIEW gate
slate gen pick --shot S05 --take t2 --by <the person who chose>
slate plates conform --shot S05            # the approved take, at the film's frame rate and size
```

- A rerun polls takes still running; it never pays twice. `--detach` runs a batch as a queued job.
- **Only a person picks.** The pick records the take's SHA-256 and locks it; the conform refuses a take that no longer
  matches the pick.
- Autonomous films ask first: `slate gen request-approval --shot S05`, then run with the approval id once the owner's yes
  is recorded.

## 4. Judge every take

At least two takes per shot, judged side by side at full size and in motion, against the brand's references. **Ugly or
AI-looking takes never ship, however much they cost.** Reject takes that drift off-look (painterly, off-hue, the wrong
sky), invent their own elements (a guide line drawn beside the film's line), or break the brief (an extra element).
Inspect interpolation on every conformed plate. See [judging takes](references/judging-takes.md).

## 5. Make it good

- **The best models by default** (from `registry.json`, pinned per film at first use), overridable per film or shot.
  See [models](references/models.md).
- **Ground every generation in the brand**: its references wired in, its tokens and rules spelled into the prompt. See
  [grounding](references/grounding.md).
- **Full visual context and long, explicit prompts** when the brand allows uploads: start and end frames, reference
  frames, the look. See [prompting](references/prompting.md).
- **Continuity across plates**: generate later plates from the film's own frames or an earlier selected plate. See
  [plates](references/plates.md).

## 6. Mattes: a generation's shape, never its pixels

Where the film's code-built world meets real footage, a generated transition can help, but its pixels on screen read
as AI. Use it as a **matte**: the generation's shape reveals real frames inside and the film's own ground outside, and
the code draws its lines and words on top. `slate plates matte --shot S05 --base <image> --real <shot>` builds it. See
[mattes](references/mattes.md).

## 7. Spend

Every call is estimated first (the estimate's `usd` is the price; `discount.usd` is only the saving), checked against
the film's budget and the month's cap, recorded in the ledger with its request id before waiting, and sent with an
Idempotency-Key, so a lost answer is resent with the same key and body and charged once. Video plates are 720p unless
the owner chooses 1080p (2.46x the price). Slate never buys credits. Higgsfield's own skills (the fast lane)
bill app credits, a separate pool that isn't funded by default. See [spend](references/spend.md).

## References

- [policy](references/policy.md): the generation setting, reasons, what's never generated, autonomous approvals.
- [prompting](references/prompting.md): full references, explicit prompts, templates per brand.
- [grounding](references/grounding.md): wiring the brand kit into every generation.
- [models](references/models.md): choosing and pinning models, routing, what the API can't do.
- [judging-takes](references/judging-takes.md): two takes or more, the review sheet, what gets rejected.
- [plates](references/plates.md): atmosphere plates, continuity, conforming, type over footage.
- [mattes](references/mattes.md): bridges as mattes over real frames.
- [spend](references/spend.md): estimates, the ledger, two wallets, costs from the first films.

# Prompting generators well

Text-only prompts had the first films' generator "flying blind": it could only make atmosphere. Given full visual context
and explicit prompts on the top models, it matched keyframes.

## Give the model everything it's allowed to see

When the brand allows uploads (`grounding.uploads_allowed`):
- **a reference pack**: the brand's look (its kit's reference frames), UI frames and reference-film frames where they
  help set the look (never to be reproduced on screen);
- **start and end frames**: the film's own frames either side of the shot, so the generation joins the film;
- **reference-to-video** inputs for continuity: an earlier selected plate, or stills from it (plates.md);
- the shot's **duration**, **aspect** and **size** (Slate fills these from film.json).

When uploads aren't allowed, the prompt carries the brand in words (grounding.md), and continuity comes from the film's
own takes, which are the film's material, not the brand's.

## Write long, explicit prompts

- Describe the shot as a cinematographer would: subject, setting, time of day, light, lens and camera movement, depth,
  colour, texture, mood, pace.
- Spell out the brand's palette tokens and rules (the colours to grade toward, what never appears).
- Say what must **not** appear: no text, no UI, no logos, no extra elements, no invented guide lines.
- One shot per prompt. Don't ask a clip to do two things.
- Keep the wording of a successful prompt as the template for the next shot of the same kind.

## Templates per brand

Plate briefs are templates, and every brand keeps its own reference pack for generations. Once a plate prompt has
produced an approved take, record it (with its model, seed and references) in the film's records and reuse it as the
starting point for the brand's next plates.

## First and last frames

- Generate **between the film's own frames**: the model then works inside the film's geometry.
- Don't hand the model background-only frames and hope it keeps the film's elements: it will draw its own versions of
  them, off by tens of pixels.
- The film's code draws its own lines and type over a plate; the generation never draws them.

## Stills

Keyframes and stills (for a plate to animate, or a look test) follow the same rules; image models vary in how they take
a palette lock, a background colour or type (never use generated type as final type).

# Models

Slate doesn't work without the best models, so the best one for each role is the default: recorded in `registry.json`
with the date it was verified, pinned per film at first use, and overridable per film (film.json `models`), per user
(`slate.toml`) or per shot (the generate block's `model`).

## Roles

The role follows from what a shot's generate block gives it:

| Role | When | Typical inputs |
|---|---|---|
| a still | no image, video or duration | a prompt |
| animate a plate | an `image` (and optionally an `end_image`), or a `duration` | a start frame, an end frame |
| style-locked from references | `reference_images` | several stills that set the look |
| extend a plate | a `video` | an earlier selected plate |

`slate plates plan` shows each shot's role, model and estimate before anything is spent.

## Routing

- **Keep a routing table and a plate review sheet.** Models differ in brief fidelity: on the first films one family came
  out painterly and off-palette, another broke the brief with an extra element, and a third matched the keyframes.
- **Resolution and length caps differ**: some video models stop at 720p; use a higher-resolution model for hero plates.
- **Availability varies**: a model can be temporarily unavailable. Have a fallback per shot.
- **Native frame rates differ** (plates often arrive at 24 fps); the conform handles it (plates.md).
- **Re-check the catalogue** at the start of a project and before assuming a gap: the catalogue changes monthly, and
  model knowledge in any agent is older than the catalogue.

## What the Cloud API can't do

- **Voice and music**: no voice or music models. Voice and music come from ElevenLabs (slate-voice, slate-sound).
- **Product-true UI or exact brand type**: generated UIs aren't the product; UI and type stay in code.
- Some app-only models and workflows (a cloud video editor, narrated explainer workflows) exist only on the app-credit
  side, which isn't funded (spend.md).

## Pinning

`slate gen run` pins a shot's model at first use. A registry refresh never changes a pinned film; re-pinning is
explicit, tested and approved, so a re-generation in week three matches week one.

# The generation policy

The owner's rule: generation is rare by default, and the person asking decides how much. Code builds anything designed;
generation is for real people, real scenes and stock-style shots code can't make, or where it genuinely adds something.
Every take is judged, and ugly or AI-looking takes never ship. The best models by default, configurable.

## The film's setting (the requester's choice)

| Setting | What may generate |
|---|---|
| `none` | nothing |
| `rarely` (default) | only what code can't make: `real-people`, `real-scene`, `stock` |
| `where-it-helps` | also `adds-something` and `bridge-matte`, each with a written `why` of at least a sentence |

Set it at intake (`slate new --generation`) from what the requester says; ask when a brief implies generated footage
("a shot of a crowded street at night") and the setting doesn't allow it.

## What's never generated

Anything designed: UI, app screens, text and type, copy, logos and wordmarks, charts and graphs, data, numbers,
diagrams, icons, brand graphics. A generate block whose `contains` lists any of these is refused: code draws it. A
generated plate is atmosphere only, with only the film's line and type over it.

## Where generation has earned its place

- **Atmosphere plates**: a landscape, weather, a city at night, where the film's world opens up.
- **Real people and real places** the film needs and can't capture or draw (with the requester's sign-off for people).
- **Stock-style shots** a film would otherwise license.
- **A bridge used as a matte** where the code's world meets real footage (mattes.md).
- **Native ambience**: some video models return usable ambience with a plate (wind and air, no music), at a small extra
  cost.

## Where it failed

- Generated pixels on screen where code or real footage existed read as AI: a generated line tracing a ridge "keeps
  floating" and was rejected; only the generation's shape survived, as a matte.
- Stylized generated explainers aren't brand work: they're stylized clips, not the brand's type or real UI.
- Background-only first and last frames made a model draw its own guide line 60 to 100 px off the film's line.

## Autonomous films

Autonomous films generate under the same rules, and every generation waits for the owner's yes:
1. `slate gen request-approval --shot <S>` writes the request (never edited afterwards) and asks the owner by iMessage and
   push (never in tests or replay).
2. The owner's yes is recorded as a spend appr
[… 7,530 characters left out of the recording …]
ed and polled.
- **A yes covers what it asked for, one call each**: an autonomous film's approval request for N takes spends as N
  slots (`<yes>#1` to `<yes>#N`), each recorded on its own ledger row, so one yes can't be spent twice. A slot whose
  call failed or was cancelled (nothing billed) is free again.
- **Cancel only reaches queued requests**; stopping polling doesn't cancel. `slate gen cancel --shot <S>` cancels properly.
- **Failed and moderated jobs aren't charged.**
- **Download outputs at once**: the vendor keeps output URLs only for a limited time. Slate does.

## Two wallets

| Wallet | Pays for | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Cloud API balance** | every Slate generation (`slate gen`) | the one funded lane |
| **App credits** | Higgsfield's CLI, app and hosted connector, including its own skills (the fast lane) and its After Effects recipes | not funded by default |

Generations made in a chat through a hosted connector bypass Slate's ledger; the session's balance snapshots catch them
(slate, budgets.md). The ElevenLabs connector's third-party image and video models bill ElevenLabs credits, and bypass the
ledger too.

**Slate never buys credits, tops up a balance or upgrades a plan.** It can say when a plan would pay for itself (the
smallest plan, one month first), and the owner decides.

## What the first films cost

| Use | Roughly |
|---|---|
| A still (keyframe or look test) | cents |
| Animating a plate, 5 seconds, on a workhorse model | about $0.25 to $1 |
| A long, high-quality plate (10 to 12 seconds on a top model) | about $11 to $15 |
| A hybrid film: about 40 s of generated plates, a few takes each | about $8 to $30 |
| An all-generated six-minute cut | roughly $55 to $95 |
| An explainer's 0 to 2 generated shots | about $15 to $30 each, including one reject |

Prices move (discounts come and go, and `registry.json`'s price notes say when each one ends); budget at list price,
and check `registry.json`'s verified-on date before a big batch.

**Resolution is a spend decision.** Video plates render at 720p by default. Seedance 2.5 also offers 1080p on every
plate workflow, at 2.46x the price (about $5.69 for a 5-second plate instead of $2.31); moving up is the owner's call,
recorded once in Slate's settings (`[gen] video_resolution`) or on one shot (`resolution` in its generate block).

# Truth research: sources you can pin and cite

A film is only as trustworthy as the sources behind it. Truth research finds what's actually true about the product
and the brand, pins each source so it can be re-checked, and records who rules on what's claimed.

## The order of authority

1. **The owner's rulings** on what's claimed. A feature can exist in the code and still be ruled out for the film
   ("that's not true" means it doesn't appear).
2. **The product's code**, read in place at a pinned commit and cited `path:line`. It wins over everything below.
3. **The brand's website, live product pages, public demos and guidelines**, read and cited with the date.
4. **Docs, prototypes, demos and older films**: layout references only. They drift: names change, numbers move,
   features are retired. When they disagree with the code, the code wins; when a product demo's wording disagrees with
   the product's code, the code wins.

For a brand the owner doesn't own, the brand's **claim authority** (a named person there) rules on claims and brand use.

**Nothing is invented**: every UI element, word and number in the film maps to a citation in the truth pack. A concept
screen (something not built) needs the requester's explicit sign-off and a visible "concept" treatment. The rules that
follow from this are in [truth packs](truth-packs.md).

## Pinning a source

Every source in `brief/truth.json` has an id and a pin: a commit, a retrieval date or a SHA-256. A claim cites a pinned
source by id, with where in it (`path:line`, a page, a section). A number with no pinned source doesn't go in the film.

```json
{
 "claim_authority": "the person who rules on this brand's claims",
 "sources": [
  {"id": "app", "title": "The product's source", "pin": "commit 3f2a9c1", "note": "read in place, never copied"},
  {"id": "site", "title": "The public website", "url": "https://example.com", "retrieved_at": "2026-09-30", "pin": "2026-09-30"}
 ],
 "claims": [
  {"id": "c1", "text": "Plans a week in one view", "source": "app", "where": "src/views/week.tsx:40"}
 ],
 "never_claim": ["works offline"],
 "sample_data": {"company": "an invented sample company, always labelled as sample data"}
}
```

## Reading company code

- Read it in place, on the machine that holds it, with read-only commands (`git show`, `git grep` at the pinned
  commit). Never copy it to another machine, into Slate, or into a prompt for a generator.
- Quote the exact copy the product uses (labels, statuses, limits) with `path:line`, and re-verify quotes before the
  build: a first pass once had to correct line numbers on about a hundred quotes.
- A voice brief or research note that quotes company code stays with the company's material; it never travels into a
  personal or public package.

## Templates

### Product truth

For a product film, write one product-truth document the builders work from:
- the pinned commit;
- the product in one paragraph;
- the journey order (how a person really goes through it);
- every screen the film shows, with its exact copy;
- the product's agent or character, if it has one;
- secondary views (partners, admins, settings);
- the product's own motion (its CSS easing tokens or its springs);
- the palette and type the film takes;
- **live versus not built**: what's shipped, what's stubbed or off by default (never shown as working);
- numbers and words to get exactly right;
- where the product disagrees with itself.

### Capability brief (for a product character or agent)

How it was checked; sources; what it knows; how it synthesizes and explains; what it suggests next; its guardrails;
**what is not true about it**; where this film differs from the product; and what the film uses. Every line carries a
source. Describe a character only with capabilities the owner treats as true.

### Reference analysis claims

When a film remakes or answers an earlier film, list every claim in the original that conflicts with the brand's
current website or product, and decide each with the claim authority before writing.

## Checking numbers

- Recheck an original's statistics against a current public source; cut or correct any that don't match.
- A figure from an older source that can't be verified goes to the claim authority before it's used.
- Percentiles, ranges and derived numbers are computed from the product's own model, not eyeballed.
- One company, one set of numbers: every shot that shows the sample reads from one sample-data record, so the same
  company never shows two different weeks.

"""From a shot's generate block to a Cloud API request body.

The block says what the shot needs in words and files; this module turns it into the model's own fields:

    {"reason": "real-scene", "why": "a real coastline at dawn", "prompt": "…", "duration": 5,
     "image": "refs/start.png", "end_image": "take:S04", "audio": true, "params": {"bitrate_mode": "high"}}

- The role (which kind of model) follows from the inputs: a `video` extends, `reference_images` guide, an `image`
  animates, and no inputs at all makes a still.
- The model is the best one for that role (registry.json) unless the film overrides it (film.json `models`, a
  pin, slate.toml or SLATE_MODEL_*), or the shot names its own. `slate gen run` pins it at first use.
- File inputs are local: a film-relative path, `take:<shot>` (another shot's approved take) or `brand:<path>` (a
  file in the brand pack). They're uploaded only at run time, and only when the brand pack allows uploads of brand
  material; estimates use a placeholder URL, since the price never depends on the picture.
- Aspect comes from film.json (the frame's ratio). Resolution: a video plate renders at its role's default in
  registry.json (720p) unless slate.toml `[gen] video_resolution` or the shot's own `resolution` says otherwise; the
  full-HD option costs 2.46x as much, so it is a person's choice (registry.json questions: plate_video_resolution). A
  still uses the film's short side, within what the model offers.
- Sound is always said out loud. Some models make native audio unless told not to (Kling 3.0 Pro's sound is on,
  Seedance 2.5's generate_audio is true), and audio costs more (a plate with sound cost 0.378 USD against 0.252
